summary:
Gauteng stands under the national constitutional framework of South Africa. The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation; the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court; the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024 explicitly protects sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics. Sexual-orientation discrimination was banned in 1996, making South Africa the first country to do so; marriage equality followed with the Civil Union Act of 2006; legal gender recognition has been available since the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003.

On 14 November 2025 the Gauteng Division of the High Court, sitting as an Equality Court, delivered judgment in Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre and Others (Case No. 2024/070075), a challenge to the Department of Correctional Services brought with the assistance of Lawyers for Human Rights. The court held that the Department had engaged in unfair discrimination and harassment of the transgender inmate by refusing to allow her to express her gender identity and by denying her prescribed gender-affirming hormone therapy, and that the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment includes gender-affirming hormonal therapy at state expense. Orders were granted compelling the Department to provide hormone treatment at state expense, permit clothing and cosmetics expressing the inmate's gender identity, implement the accommodations required by its own standard operating procedure for transgender inmates, and deliver prescribed medical care. The South African Human Rights Commission's National Preventive Mechanism welcomed the ruling the same day.

The Mokoena judgment is the only documented determination of where transgender prisoners are housed in Gauteng. Mokoena, a transgender woman serving a life sentence, is held at Johannesburg Correctional Centre. She was initially housed in Medium A section, where she could express her gender identity through long hair, makeup and women's clothing, and was later transferred to Medium C section. At the time of the judgment she was housed in C Single Section, a segregated unit of Medium C associated with solitary confinement, and despite requesting a single cell she was accommodated with cisgender male cellmates. The court found that the Department's own standard operating procedures prescribe accommodation appropriate to gender identity where feasible and safe, that no basis existed for refusing her a single cell, and ordered the Department to house her in a single cell or with inmates of the same gender identity and to enforce its transgender-inmate procedures.

Correctional Services already had a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners before the ruling. Reporting in August 2025 recorded that rights organisations doubt whether it is implemented in practice. Detention therefore remains a site of elevated risk for trans visitors and residents in Gauteng despite the binding remedies now in force.

Violence against trans people in the province is documented and ongoing. On 26 December 2024 Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old transgender woman originally from Soshanguve and living in Winterveld, both in the Tshwane area of Gauteng, was assaulted at a local tavern at about 1:30 am after a man began saying gay and lesbian people 'don't deserve to live'. He smashed a bottle into her face as she lit a cigarette, saying 'I told you I'm gonna kill you', leaving deep cuts to her mouth, lips, nose, cheek and forehead that were stitched after treatment at Kgabo Clinic. She opened an assault case at Dube Police Station, which MambaOnline reported on 6 January 2025 had shown no progress. OUT LGBT Well-being's rights watch for December 2024 recorded five LGBTQIA+ murders that month. Violence disproportionately affects Black lesbian, trans and gender-nonconforming people in townships.

Outside detention, everyday exposure is shaped by documents. The Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act requires medical evidence, a pathologising route that locks people out of legal gender recognition, and its binary sex classification excludes non-binary people altogether; reform toward self-determination is pending but not in force. The cost of affirming one's gender through the process is described as dauntingly high. Where identity documents do not match presentation, trans people face humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for alleged fraud. A 2024 Gender Dynamix report documents a trans woman who was met with police mockery and refused when she attempted to file a domestic-violence complaint after producing her identity document.

Access to gender-affirming care across South Africa is uneven. Activists in East London delivered a memorandum to Frere Hospital over treatment delays running to a year, a non-Gauteng case that illustrates the national gap between entitlement and service delivery. Academic analysis published in 2024 on whether PEPUDA read with section 9 of the Constitution prohibits the exclusion of transgender and non-binary people from gender-segregated bathrooms concludes that trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in facility access, so restroom and changing-room disputes remain foreseeable for visitors.
tangentialFactors:
Gauteng carries the densest hate-crime evidence base in South Africa, though the studies are oriented to gay and lesbian victims rather than trans people specifically. 'Hate Crimes Against Gay and Lesbian People in Gauteng: Prevalence, Consequences and Contributing Factors', a 2003/04 Joint Working Group research initiative conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being with the University of South Africa's Centre for Applied Psychology (authors Wells and Polders), is the first representative quantitative provincial hate-crime study conducted anywhere in the country; its partner roster included Behind the Mask, Triangle Project, the Gay and Lesbian Memory in Action archive and the Durban Lesbian and Gay Community and Health Centre.

The 2016 Love Not Hate campaign research hosted by the Gay and Lesbian Memory in Action archive and conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being confirms that only three quantitative hate-crime studies have ever been done in South Africa: the 2003 empowerment study covering Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal and the Western Cape, a 2010 North West province study, and the national campaign study itself. The 2016 work also measures discrimination against LGBT people nationally. The provincial evidence base is therefore real but thin, and no province-specific enforcement action or ban on trans people exists in Gauteng; the constitutional and statutory protections operate uniformly across South Africa.

Legal gender recognition in Gauteng sits behind the same pathologising statutory route that applies nationwide, and reform is pending without being in force, so provincial courts operate under the pre-reform binary classification. Care-delivery gaps documented in other provinces show that the Equality Court remedy obtained in Mokoena has not resolved uneven treatment access elsewhere in the country.
localsOnly:
Residents of Gauteng who are unable to bring identity documents into line with presentation face documented humiliation, refusal of service and threats of arrest for alleged fraud. The Gender Dynamix report of 2024 records one trans woman being mocked by police and refused assistance when she attempted to file a domestic-violence complaint after producing her identity document, indicating that the failure is not confined to private service providers.

Legal gender recognition remains available only through the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act route, which requires medical evidence, carries costs described as dauntingly high, and recognises only a binary sex classification, excluding non-binary people from the process entirely. Reform toward self-determination has been proposed but is not law.

Correctional Services maintains a standard operating procedure for transgender inmates, but the Mokoena orders required the Department to enforce it as well as to house the applicant in a single cell or with inmates of the same gender identity, and the SOP's existence pre-dated the judgment. Rights organisations reported in August 2025 that they doubt implementation in practice.

Enforcement of police duties toward trans complainants remains uneven. Assault and hate-crime cases can be opened, as Mokoena-style reporting shows in the Mahlobo case, but the reported outcome of the December 2024 tavern assault case at Dube Police Station had not progressed as of 6 January 2025. The Equality Court route under PEPUDA and the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment, including gender-affirming hormonal therapy at state expense, are the operative protections residents can invoke.
outOfScopeNotes:
The delivery date of the Mokoena judgment is stated inconsistently across sources: the source inventory dates it 14 November 2025, while the South African Human Rights Commission statement quoted within the same inventory records the judgment as delivered on 10 November 2025. The discrepancy is unresolved here; the operative orders and findings are consistent across sources.

Whether the Department of Correctional Services' standard operating procedure for transgender inmates is implemented in practice in Gauteng is not established. Rights organisations expressed doubt in August 2025 reporting, but no independent audit of facility-level compliance is available for this jurisdiction.

No quantified data is sourced on the volume of trans-specific hate-crime reports in Gauteng, on police clearance rates for such cases, or on Equality Court outcomes brought under PEPUDA by trans complainants in the province beyond the single Mokoena determination. The provincial hate-crime studies in the inventory concern gay and lesbian victims in 2003/04 and do not isolate transgender complainants.

The current status of the pending reform to the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act, including any provincial legislative or administrative measures taken in Gauteng toward self-determination, is not sourced. The claim that the process's costs are 'dauntingly high' appears in the parent framework without a provincial cost figure, and no comparative cost data for Gauteng is available here.

Whether gender-affirming care in Gauteng hospitals is subject to the year-long treatment delays documented at Frere Hospital in the Eastern Cape is not stated in the sources; the non-Gauteng case is used only to indicate national unevenness. Similarly, the 2024 academic analysis on gender-segregated bathrooms is national in scope, and no Gauteng-specific dispute or enforcement outcome is sourced.
